leads.name: Mesto de las Rozas
leads.blocked_reason: Known dead. This is Montalban de Cordoba's 'Mesto de las Rozas', a Quercus ilex x Quercus suber natural hybrid in the Las Rozas area (Campina Cordobesa), about 7km from the town (approx. municipality centre 37.5477, -4.7430; no tree-level coordinate exists or is needed now). es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesto_de_las_Rozas (fetched directly) states the trunk split and the whole crown fell in a severe storm in summer 1995; only the trunk and a regrowth shoot remain on site. The one photo we hold, File:Elmesto.jpg, is captioned on Commons 'El Mesto de las Rozas. Anos 80' (the tree in the 1980s), i.e. it depicts the tree BEFORE it fell, not a current living specimen; publishing it as a photo of a living tree would misrepresent a historical image as current. The brief's guess that 'Mesto' was an Asturias/Cantabria term was wrong; it is a Cordoba/Andalusia hybrid-oak name and this is a different region entirely from the other three candidates in this batch. Hard rule: never publish a tree known to be dead. This can appear only as historical context inside a story about the region, never as a collectible entry. Verification pass 2026-09-27.

leads.species: Spanish Black Pine (Pinus nigra subsp. salzmannii)

leads.verify_note: 2026-09-27 verification pass: Pino del Aprisquillo, La Adrada, Avila. Spain's Tree of the Year 2016, European Tree of the Year 2017 finalist. Four sources agree on species and general dimensions (girth 500-590cm, height 25-30m per three sources, one outlier at 43m), age given vaguely as 'about 400 years' / '350 years' across sources. Location confirmed via a geotagged, provincial-government-credited Commons photo matching this lead's own coordinate exactly. 85km from Madrid, no public transport, standalone single-famous-tree candidate.

leads.name: Olmo de Navajas
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.verify_note: 2026-09-27 verification pass: Olmo de Navajas, Plaza del Olmo, Navajas, Castellon. Spain's Tree of the Year 2019. Three sources agree: planted 1636 (documented planting date for this specimen, not a bridge claim), girth ~630-650cm, height disputed (13.87m vs 19m across sources, flagged), notably unaffected by Dutch elm disease. Location confirmed to five decimals by both a geotagged Commons photo and this tree's own dedicated Wikidata item (Q105762033). 47km from Valencia with no fast transit link; standalone single-famous-tree candidate, strongest-pinned of the batch.

leads.name: Pino-roble de Canicosa de la Sierra
leads.species: Pyrenean Oak (Quercus pyrenaica) with a Scots Pine (Pinus sylvestris) growing from its hollow trunk
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.verify_note: 2026-09-27 verification pass: Pino-Roble de Canicosa de la Sierra, Burgos. A living oak/pine symbiosis (pine germinated inside the oak's hollow trunk), not a single tree; treated as one collectible ensemble. Fifth place, European Tree of the Year 2016. Four sources agree on ages (oak ~250yr, pine ~130yr) and the formation story; the most detailed source (canicosa.info) gives oak girth 340cm, pine girth 200cm at 2.9m, and notes the oak is in active decline with no conservation measures, i.e. alive but genuinely fragile. Location confirmed within ~100m by two independent GPS fixes. No cluster or nearby published city; standalone single-famous-tree candidate on rarity/story rather than size.
